title: Built a playable 3D browser game in one evening using Opus 5 + Codex (WebGL / Three.js)
author: RemarkableCaramel483
selftext:
I’ve been experimenting with **Opus 5 + Codex** for game development, and I honestly didn’t expect to get this far in a single evening.

The result is a small playable prototype called **Alice’s Tea Party World**, built with **WebGL + Three.js**.

It’s still very early and there’s a lot to polish, but I wanted to share the progress because the development workflow felt completely different from anything I’ve used before.

A few things that surprised me:

* Most of the repetitive Three.js boilerplate disappeared.
* Iterating on gameplay ideas became much faster.
* I could spend more time experimenting with mechanics instead of wiring everything together.
* The AI wasn’t writing the whole game for me, but it dramatically sped up prototyping.

The current prototype includes:

* A stylized 3D Alice in Wonderland-inspired environment
* Browser-based rendering (WebGL / Three.js)
* Basic gameplay interactions
* A playable vertical slice

Here’s a short recording from tonight’s build.

I’d also love to hear from other people using AI for game development.

* What’s your current workflow?
* Are you using Codex, Claude/Opus, Cursor, or something else?
* Where do you think AI helps the most in game development, and where does it still struggle?

Feedback is very welcome!

comments.author: Additional_Poet9207
comments.body:
As an “artist” (let’s say), I can say that right now coding is the only field where I’m genuinely comfortable with heavy AI assistance. Mainly because it still lets you focus on the idea itself and on designing the game’s mechanics.  
Secondly, I’m genuinely surprised that all of this wasn’t built around highly assets, and I definitely share everyone else’s curiosity about that!  
Lastly, I’m also starting to explore this world myself. For now, though, I’ve chosen a hybrid approach because I need to understand (kind of) what I’m doing as I go. To keep it simple, I give my ideas to Claude, and it explains exactly what I should do and, more importantly, why I should do it. It’s an unnecessarily slow process, but it makes me feel much more aware of what I’m building.  
Congratulations again.

replies.author: RemarkableCaramel483
replies.body: Thanks, really appreciate it! I actually like that approach too. AI is great at speeding things up, but understanding *why* something works is still incredibly valuable. That’s also why we kept most of the assets handmade—we wanted to focus on using AI to accelerate development and iteration, not replace the creative decisions. Good luck with your project! 😊

replies.author: Potential-Bend7214
replies.body:
I decided to answer the last 3 questions at the end. usually my workflow is something like this:

\-ask the ai a prompt and request it to make md files for critical decisions, guidelines, requirements, etc depending on whatever I need

\-then I slowly add on when I need something, requesting it to always update and follow each and every md file until I get the result I like

i use antigravity, more favorably Claude (opus or sonnet. I use sonnet for bugs and opus for massive graphic updates and editing). 

I think AI helps with boilerplate and repetition in code, specifically in HTML and CSS. I don’t really need to explain why. But the vibecoded buttons (gradients, floating, glowing, etc) and graphics definitely could improve when it comes to ai coding, which is why most ai game devs use meshy to import 3d models or ask Claude to do voxel art, which is easier than flat ai images or weird animations since that isn’t what code ai specializes in.

Love the game so far btw
